title: Training masters athletes
goal: Describe how well older athletes still adapt to training, and apply the points on intensity, strength, protein, recovery and bone health.

steps.title: Older bodies still adapt
steps.text:
Older people respond to training. A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials in 480 adults aged 65 or over found that both interval and continuous training raised VO₂peak compared with no training, and intervals did more [[c:bouaziz]]. Over no training, the gain from intervals was about 3.4 times the gain from continuous training (pooled mean differences 4.61 against 1.35), and intervals also won when the two were compared head to head.

These are trials in seniors in general, not masters athletes: a trained masters athlete starts higher and has less room to gain. And the review of lifelong athletes says high-intensity training can be held for about a decade at best [[c:hawk]].

claims.text: In adults aged 65 or over, interval training raised VO₂peak more than continuous training, and both more than no training.

evidence.quote: High-intensity interval training and ET both elicit large improvements in the VO2peak of older adults aged 65 or over. When compared with ET, the gain in VO2peak was greater following HIIT.
VO2peak was significantly higher after ET sessions compared with controls (mean difference-MD = 1.35; 95% confidence interval-CI: 0.73-1.96)
compared HIIT with controls (MD = 4.61; 95% CI: 3.21-6.01), but also when compared HIIT with ET (MD = 3.76; 95% CI: 2.96-4.56)

claims.text: Maintaining high-intensity training seems limited to about one decade at best and to a select few people.

evidence.quote: maintaining high-intensity training seems limited to approximately one decade at best and to a select few individuals

steps.title: Keep some hard work
steps.text:
Intensity is the first thing masters athletes lose: injury, work and family, and lower motivation all push it down [[c:why]]. A review said lower intensity and volume of training explain much of the fall in performance [[c:tr]]. Intervals are also the type of training that gained most in older adults (previous card).

One change matters for zones. Maximal heart rate falls with age whatever you do. A fixed 220 − age rule drifts: at 60 it gives 160, while 208 − 0.7 × age gives 166, and people differ from either by about 11 beats·min⁻¹. If you set heart rate zones, anchor them to a measured maximum.

claims.text: Injuries, job and family demands and lower motivation probably contribute to masters athletes' reduced training intensity and volume.

evidence.quote: Increased prevalence of exercise training-associated injuries among Masters athletes also probably contributes to their reduced training intensity and volume
Increases in job- and family-related responsibilities may impinge on the availability of time and energy for the intensive training required to remain competitive
the motivation to train may be reduced with advancing age among Masters athletes

claims.text: The fall in endurance performance with ageing appears mediated in large part by lower training intensity and volume.

evidence.quote: appear to be mediated in large part by a reduction in the intensity (velocity) and volume of the exercise that can be performed during training sessions

steps.title: Strength training
steps.text:
Heavy lifting works at older age. A meta-analysis of 47 studies (1,079 people aged 50 or over) found strength gains of 24–33% across four lifts, larger with higher intensity [[c:pet]]. For masters endurance athletes, 3 weeks of knee-extension training raised strength by 17.8% (young athletes 5.9%), and cycling [delta efficiency](g:delta-efficiency) rose in the masters [[c:louis]]. Masters marathon runners seem to benefit from adding strength work too [[c:pia]].

Keeping the gains costs more. After 16 weeks of lifting, cutting the dose to a third kept muscle growth in young adults but not in people aged 60–75, though their strength gains held [[c:bickel]]. The strength lessons cover programming.

claims.text: Resistance exercise improves strength in adults aged 50 and over, more with higher intensity.

evidence.quote: RE is effective for improving strength among older adults, particularly with higher intensity training.

claims.text: Three weeks of knee-extension strength training raised strength more in masters (+17.8%) than in young endurance athletes (+5.9%) and improved cycling delta efficiency in the masters.

evidence.quote: The strength training induced a significant improvement in MVC torque in all the subjects, more pronounced in masters (+17.8% in masters vs. +5.9% in young, P < 0.05).

claims.text: Master endurance runners seem to benefit from concurrent strength and endurance training.

evidence.quote: master endurance athletes seem to benefit from concurrent strength and endurance training

claims.text: Both maintenance doses kept muscle growth in young adults but not in older adults, who need a higher weekly dose; strength gains were well kept in the older adults.

evidence.quote: Both maintenance prescriptions preserved phase 1 muscle hypertrophy in the young but not the old.

older adults require a higher dose of weekly loading than the young to maintain myofiber hypertrophy attained during a progressive RT program, yet gains in specific strength among older adults were well preserved

steps.title: Recovery and protein
steps.text:
Do older athletes recover more slowly? Many believe so, but a review found it hard to say: studies rarely separate age from lower activity, and often use exercise unlike normal training [[c:fell]]. Treat recovery time as individual and track it with the load and HRV lessons.

Protein is clearer. A position paper for people over 65 asks for at least 1.0–1.2 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹, and at least 1.2 for those who exercise [[c:bauer]]. The previous lesson suggested older men may need about 0.40 g·kg⁻¹ in one meal against 0.24 in young men. Daily totals and meal sizes are in the protein lessons for younger athletes.

claims.text: It is unclear whether ageing slows recovery from exercise, because studies rarely separate age from lower activity or use realistic training.

evidence.quote: This makes it difficult to differentiate the respective roles of declining physical activity and aging on the recovery process.

claims.text: People over 65 who exercise should have at least 1.2 g protein per kg per day.

evidence.quote: higher protein intake (ie, ≥ 1.2 g/kg body weight/d) is advised for those who are exercising and otherwise active

steps.title: Bone health
steps.text:
Bone thins with age, and some masters athletes start thin. In a review, regular road cyclists had low [bone density](g:bone-mineral-density) at key sites such as the lumbar spine, and road cycling gave no clear bone benefit [[c:olm]]. The bone lessons explain why.

Heavy lifting with impact helps. In the LIFTMOR trial, postmenopausal women with low bone mass did supervised sessions of 5 sets of 5 reps above 85% of one-repetition maximum ([1RM](g:repetition-maximum)) twice a week for 8 months. Lumbar-spine density rose 2.9% against −1.2% in controls [[c:wat]]. Men with low bone mass gained 4.1%, against 0.9% in non-randomised controls and 2.0% on a machine-based programme [[c:har]]. In the 20-year study, older athletes who lifted had better arm bone density [[c:pol]].

claims.text: Adult road cyclists in regular training have low bone density at key sites such as the lumbar spine; road cycling does not appear to confer any significant osteogenic benefit.

evidence.quote: From our comprehensive survey of the current available literature it can be concluded that road cycling does not appear to confer any significant osteogenic benefit.

claims.text: In postmenopausal women with low bone mass, supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training raised lumbar-spine bone density by 2.9% against −1.2% in controls.

evidence.quote: HiRIT (n = 49) effects were superior to CON (n = 52) for lumbar spine (LS) BMD (2.9 ± 2.8% versus -1.2 ± 2.8%, p < 0.001)
randomized to either 8 months of twice-weekly, 30-minute, supervised HiRIT (5 sets of 5 repetitions, >85% 1 repetition maximum) or a home-based, low-intensity exercise program (CON)

claims.text: In men with low bone mass, high-intensity resistance and impact training raised lumbar-spine bone density by 4.1%, against 0.9% in a non-randomised control group and 2.0% with machine-based isometric training.

evidence.quote: HiRIT improved trochanteric BMD (2.8 ± 0.8%; -0.1 ± 0.9%, p = .024), LS BMD (4.1 ± 0.7%; 0.9 ± 0.8%, p = .003)
HiRIT improved LS BMD (4.1 ± 0.7%; 2.0 ± 0.7%, p = .039)

claims.text: Older athletes who did weight training had greater arm bone mineral density than those who did not.

evidence.quote: Those who performed weight training had a greater arm region bone mineral density than those who did not.

points: Older adults still gain VO₂peak from training, and intervals gain more than continuous work; trained athletes have less room.
Intensity is what masters athletes drop first; keep some, and anchor heart rate zones to a measured maximum.
Heavy strength training works at older age, and older adults need a higher weekly dose to keep the gains.
Older athletes need more protein (at least 1.2 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹); whether recovery is slower from ageing itself is unclear.
Road cycling gives little bone benefit; supervised heavy lifting with impact raised spine density in low-bone-mass groups.

variants.stem: In the meta-analysis of adults aged 65 or over, which training raised VO₂peak the most?

options.text: High-intensity intervals
options.why: Right: intervals beat both continuous training and no training.

options.text: Continuous moderate training
options.why: It helped, but its gain over controls was under a third of the interval gain.

options.text: Neither: older adults do not adapt
options.why: Both types raised VO₂peak above controls.

options.text: They did equally well
options.why: Intervals also beat continuous training when the two were compared directly.

variants.stem: A 62-year-old who has raced for 30 years reads this meta-analysis. What most limits how far its VO₂peak gains apply to them?

options.text: It covered seniors in general; athletes start higher with less to gain
options.why: Right: trained athletes may gain less than the pooled seniors.

options.text: Randomised trials cannot show effects of training
options.why: Randomised trials are the strongest design for this question.

options.text: Interval training works only in young people
options.why: It raised VO₂peak in those aged 65 and over.

options.text: It pooled too many trials to be reliable
options.why: Pooling 15 trials strengthens the result.

variants.stem: A 60-year-old sets his top heart rate zone from 220 − age = 160. A lab test shows a maximum of 171. What happens to his hard intervals?

options.text: His "maximal" zone is too low, so intervals are easier than planned
options.why: Right: the real maximum is 11 beats·min⁻¹ above the formula, and the formula underestimates in older adults.

options.text: They are too hard, because the real maximum is lower
options.why: The real maximum is higher, not lower.

options.text: Nothing changes: zones do not depend on the maximum
options.why: Zones set as a share of HRmax move with it.

options.text: They are correct because 220 − age is exact
options.why: The formula is an average, with a spread of about 11 beats·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: Why do many masters athletes train less hard than at 40?

options.text: Older muscle cannot do interval work at all
options.why: Older adults gain most from intervals in trials.

options.text: Injuries, work and family demands and lower motivation all play a part
options.why: Right: these are the reasons the review gives.

options.text: Maximal heart rate rises, so easy training feels hard
options.why: Maximal heart rate falls with age.

options.text: Older athletes no longer adapt to any training
options.why: They do adapt, only less.

variants.stem: A 28-year-old and a 66-year-old both lifted 3 days a week for 16 weeks, then cut to one third of that dose for 32 weeks. What does the trial predict for muscle growth?

options.text: The young keep their gain; the older lose some
options.why: Right: the older group needed a higher weekly dose to keep muscle growth.

options.text: Both keep it
options.why: Only the young kept the muscle growth.

options.text: Both lose it
options.why: The young kept it at that dose.

options.text: The older gain more, as they have more to gain
options.why: They did not; they lost the hypertrophy at that dose.

variants.stem: The knee-extension study found masters gained 17.8% in strength against 5.9% in young athletes, with 9 masters and 8 young over 3 weeks. How much weight can this bear?

options.text: Little: a small group and a short period, with no control group
options.why: Right: it is a single-group trial with 17 people, so it is only a hint.

options.text: A lot: a difference of 12 points in 3 weeks is proof of a lasting effect
options.why: Small, short studies cannot show lasting effects.

options.text: None: strength cannot be tested in masters
options.why: Strength was measured as maximal voluntary torque.

options.text: A lot: it is a randomised trial with a control group
options.why: It had no control group.

variants.stem: A 75 kg runner aged 68 trains daily. What is the least daily protein the position paper advises?

options.why: Right: 1.2 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ × 75 kg = 90 g.
That uses 1.0 g·kg⁻¹, the bound for older people who do not exercise.
That divides 75 by 1.2 instead of multiplying.
That uses 2.0 g·kg⁻¹, a young-athlete figure not in this paper.

variants.stem: A 62 kg runner aged 70 trains daily. What is the least daily protein the position paper advises?

options.why: That uses 1.0 g·kg⁻¹, the bound for older people who do not exercise.
That divides 62 by 1.2 instead of multiplying.
That uses 2.0 g·kg⁻¹, a young-athlete figure not in this paper.

variants.stem: An 84 kg cyclist aged 66 trains daily. What is the least daily protein the position paper advises?

options.why: That uses 1.0 g·kg⁻¹, the bound for older people who do not exercise.
That divides 84 by 1.2 instead of multiplying.
That uses 2.0 g·kg⁻¹, a young-athlete figure not in this paper.

variants.stem: Why can't the review say that ageing itself slows recovery in athletes?

options.text: Studies rarely separate age from lower activity, and use unrealistic exercise
options.why: Right: that is the review's limit.

options.text: Older athletes recover just as fast in every study
options.why: The review says the evidence is unclear, not that recovery is equal.

options.text: Recovery cannot be measured
options.why: Studies measure muscle damage and repair; the design is the issue.

options.text: Young athletes were not studied
options.why: The problem is the match of activity level and exercise type.

variants.stem: A 64-year-old road cyclist rides 12 hours a week and a scan shows low lumbar-spine bone density. Which addition has the best support?

options.text: Supervised heavy lifting and impact work, twice weekly
options.why: Right: the LIFTMOR programme raised spine density in people with low bone mass.

options.text: Adding more hours on the bike each week
options.why: Road cycling gives no clear bone benefit, so more hours do not fix it.

options.text: Swimming sessions for fitness and recovery
options.why: Swimming, like cycling, is not weight-bearing.

options.text: A daily calcium supplement and nothing else
options.why: The trials tested loading, not supplements alone.

variants.stem: LIFTMOR included supervised women, about 65, with low bone mass. What most limits applying it to a fit 60-year-old man with normal bone density?

options.text: Participants had low bone mass and were supervised
options.why: Right: the groups and supervision differ from this man's case.

options.text: It was not randomised, so the result is worthless
options.why: The women's trial was randomised and the men's was semi-randomised; both inform the question.

options.text: Heavy lifting is unsafe at any age
options.why: The programmes were supervised and built up step by step, which was part of what was tested.

options.text: Lumbar spine density cannot be measured
options.why: It was measured with DXA scans.
